lead: A bar pulled in tension gets longer and also thinner. Two changes happen at once. Volumetric strain measures both together: it is the fractional change in volume of the material, ΔV/V₀. Designers need it because a bush pressed into a housing, a rubber pad in a bridge bearing, or a part inside a deep-sea housing must not change size too much. This chapter shows how the three normal strains add up to a volume change, and how Poisson's ratio decides whether the volume grows, stays the same, or shrinks.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for E, K and Poisson's ratio, and Chapter 1.1 for normal stress.

blocks.text: Take a small rectangular block with sides a, b and c along the x, y and z axes. Its original volume is V₀ = a × b × c. Under load each side changes: a becomes a + Δa, and so on. When the strains are small, the new volume works out to V₀(1 + ε_x + ε_y + ε_z). Terms such as ε_x ε_y are products of two small numbers and are dropped.
ε_v = ΔV / V₀ = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z
blocks.where: ε_v is the volumetric strain (no units); ΔV is the change in volume, in mm³ or m³; V₀ is the original volume, in the same unit; ε_x, ε_y, ε_z are the normal strains along the three axes, each no units.

blocks.text: This sum is also called dilation. It is dimensionless. A value of 0.0002 means the volume grew by 0.02 per cent. Positive ε_v means expansion, negative means contraction. Because it is only a sum of normal strains, shear strains do not enter: a pure shear distorts the shape of the block but does not change its volume in small-strain theory.

items: Find the normal stress in each of the three directions, using loads and areas.
Convert each stress to a strain with Hooke's law, allowing for the sideways pull of the other two stresses.
Add the three strains. The total is ε_v.
Multiply by the original volume to get ΔV.

blocks.text: The small-strain step matters. Once a rubber part doubles in length, or a metal part passes yield, products of strains are no longer negligible and the simple sum fails. Everything here assumes strains well below one per cent, which covers most machine parts in service.

Pull a bar with axial stress σ along x, with the other faces free. Hooke's law gives ε_x = σ/E. The two lateral directions are unloaded, so the bar contracts there by Poisson's ratio: ε_y = ε_z = −νσ/E. Adding the three:

blocks.where: σ is the axial stress in N/mm² (MPa); E is Young's modulus in N/mm²; ν is Poisson's ratio, no units; ε_v is the volumetric strain.

blocks.text: The bracket (1 − 2ν) decides everything. Steel with ν = 0.30 gives a bracket of 0.40: at σ = 200 MPa and E = 200 GPa, ε_v = 0.001 × 0.40 = 0.0004, so the bar gains 0.04 per cent in volume while it stretches. Cork has ν close to zero, so the bracket is close to 1 and it changes volume almost as much as it stretches — that is why a cork stopper stays gripped in a bottle neck. Rubber has ν close to 0.5, so the bracket is close to zero: stretch it a lot and its volume barely moves.

At ν = 0.5 exactly, ε_v is zero and the material is called incompressible. No ordinary elastic material goes above 0.5. The volume change of a whole bar is ΔV = ε_v × V₀, valid while the stress is uniform along the bar. Compression is the same formula with σ negative: ε_v comes out negative and the volume falls. If the stress varies along the length, the bar must be cut into slices and the changes added — see Chapter 1.6.
A useful number: for steel, ε_v is only about 40 per cent of ε_x. The length grows faster than the volume, which is exactly why a wire stretches without swelling.

Now press the block equally on all six faces with pressure p. Put σ_x = σ_y = σ_z = −p into the generalised Hooke's law, ε_x = (1/E)[σ_x − ν(σ_y + σ_z)]. Each strain becomes −p(1 − 2ν)/E, and all three are equal. Adding them:
ε_v = − p / K    with    K = E / [3(1 − 2ν)]
blocks.where: p is the hydrostatic pressure in N/mm² (MPa), positive when it pushes inward; K is the bulk modulus in N/mm²; E is Young's modulus in N/mm²; ν is Poisson's ratio; ε_v is the volumetric strain.

blocks.text: K measures resistance to volume change, not to shape change. A fluid with large K needs a big pressure to be squeezed. The relation K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)] is one of the standard links between the elastic constants given in Chapter 1.4. As ν approaches 0.5, K approaches infinity and the material refuses to change volume.

Watch the sign. Pressure p is positive inward, so ε_v comes out negative: the volume shrinks. Water has K about 2.2 GPa, so a pressure of 2.2 MPa squeezes it by about 0.1 per cent. Steel has K about 160 GPa, some seventy times stiffer in volume than water. Oil is preferred in hydraulic systems because it lubricates the moving parts and prevents corrosion.

figure.caption: Axial stress gives one extension strain and two lateral contractions. Adding the three gives a volumetric strain of 2.4×10⁻⁴ for the bar in the worked example.

spec.title: Volumetric strain
spec.aria: An axial stress of 120 MPa produces one extension strain of 6×10⁻⁴ and two lateral contraction strains of −1.8×10⁻⁴ each, whose sum is a volumetric strain of 2.4×10⁻⁴.

examples.question: A steel bar of square cross-section 20 mm × 20 mm and length 1.2 m carries an axial tensile load of 48 kN. Take E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.30. Find the axial stress, the three normal strains, the volumetric strain and the change in volume.
steps: Axial stress σ = P/A = 48000 N ÷ 400 mm² = 120 N/mm² = 120 MPa.
Volumetric strain ε_v = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z = 6×10⁻⁴ − 1.8×10⁻⁴ − 1.8×10⁻⁴ = 2.4×10⁻⁴. Check with the formula: ε_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2ν) = 6×10⁻⁴ × (1 − 0.60) = 2.4×10⁻⁴.
Original volume V₀ = A × L = 400 mm² × 1200 mm = 480000 mm³ = 4.8×10⁻⁴ m³.
Change in volume ΔV = ε_v × V₀ = 2.4×10⁻⁴ × 480000 mm³ = 115.2 mm³, that is 1.152×10⁻⁷ m³.
examples.answer: The volumetric strain is 2.4×10⁻⁴ (0.024 per cent) and the bar gains 115.2 mm³ of volume.
examples.check:
d = 20.0
L = 1200.0
P = 48000.0
E = 200000.0
nu = 0.30
A = d*d
sigma = P/A
eps_x = sigma/E
eps_v = eps_x*(1 - 2*nu)
V0 = A*L
dV = eps_v*V0
print(round(sigma, 6))
print(round(eps_x, 10))
print(round(eps_v, 10))
print(round(dV, 6))

traps: Adding three equal axial strains σ/E and forgetting that two of them are lateral and negative — the answer comes out several times too large.
A sign slip on the lateral strains: using +νσ/E gives ε_v = (σ/E)(1 + 2ν) instead of (1 − 2ν).
Using ν = 0.5 for a normal metal and getting zero volume change.
For ν close to 0.5, K comes out very large — that is correct, not an error; report it as nearly incompressible.
Mixing units: σ in MPa with E in GPa. Divide 120 by 200000, not by 200.
Writing ΔV = ε_v × V where V is the final volume. Use the original volume V₀; for the small strains here the two differ by a negligible amount, but the definition uses V₀.

quiz.q: Define volumetric strain and give its symbol and units.
quiz.a: Volumetric strain ε_v is the change in volume divided by the original volume, ε_v = ΔV/V₀. It is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Write ε_v for a block in terms of the three normal strains, and state the assumption used.
quiz.a: ε_v = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z. The strains must be small, so that products such as ε_x ε_y can be neglected.

quiz.q: Why do shear strains not appear in the expression for volumetric strain?
quiz.a: A shear strain changes the angles of the block but not its side lengths to first order, so the volume is unchanged. Only the three normal strains alter the volume.

quiz.q: A material has Poisson's ratio 0.5. What happens to its volume under axial tension, and what is its bulk modulus?
quiz.a: ε_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2ν) = 0, so the volume stays constant; the material is incompressible. K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)] becomes infinite.

quiz.q: A bar of E = 100 GPa and ν = 0.25 is under axial stress 80 MPa. Find the volumetric strain.
A component is under hydrostatic pressure 5 MPa. Take K = 2 GPa. Find the volumetric strain and say whether the volume grows or shrinks.
quiz.a: ε_v = −p/K = −5/2000 = −0.0025. The strain is negative, so the volume falls by 0.25 per cent.

quiz.q: Two bars have the same σ, E and volume but ν = 0.30 and ν = 0.45. Which changes volume more, and by what ratio?
quiz.a: Brackets are 1 − 0.60 = 0.40 and 1 − 0.90 = 0.10. The bar with ν = 0.30 changes volume four times as much.

quiz.q: A rubber band is stretched to twice its length and its cross-section shrinks. Explain why its density hardly changes.
quiz.a: Rubber is nearly incompressible (ν ≈ 0.5), so the length doubling is matched by the cross-sectional area halving and the volume, hence the density, hardly changes. The linear formula ε_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2ν) is only the small-strain statement of this.

beyond: Not for the exam. Engineers who study soils use the same idea under the name consolidation: a load on saturated clay squeezes water out and the skeleton compacts, and the compressibility of the pore water sets the time scale. Metal foams and some engineered lattice structures are made with a negative Poisson's ratio; they widen sideways when stretched and can swell in volume, and they are used in energy absorbers. Finite element software warns about volumetric locking in nearly incompressible rubbers, which is the same difficulty as ν approaching 0.5. Search next for the terms bulk modulus, dilation, poroelasticity and hyperelasticity.
